claim: Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are proton-gated cation channels that are involved in diverse neuronal processes including pain sensing.
source: Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are proton-gated cation channels that are involved in diverse neuronal processes including pain sensing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: The peptide toxin Mambalgin1 (Mamba1) from black mamba snake venom can reversibly inhibit the conductance of ASICs, causing an analgesic effect.
source: The peptide toxin Mambalgin1 (Mamba1) from black mamba snake venom can reversibly inhibit the conductance of ASICs, causing an analgesic effect.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on Mambalgin1.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of human ASIC1a (hASIC1a) was resolved at 3.56 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present single-particle cryo-EM structures of human ASIC1a (hASIC1a) and the hASIC1a-Mamba1 complex at resolutions of 3.56 and 3.90 Å, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from cryo-EM structure determination reported in the manuscript.

claim: The cryo-EM structure of the hASIC1a-Mamba1 complex was resolved at 3.90 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present single-particle cryo-EM structures of human ASIC1a (hASIC1a) and the hASIC1a-Mamba1 complex at resolutions of 3.56 and 3.90 Å, respectively.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data from cryo-EM structure determination reported in the manuscript.

claim: Mamba1 preferentially binds hASIC1a in a closed state.
source: The combination of the structural and physiological data indicates that Mamba1 preferentially binds hASIC1a in a closed state and reduces the proton sensitivity of the channel, representing a closed-state trapping mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by both structural data from cryo-EM and electrophysiological measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mamba1 reduces the proton sensitivity of hASIC1a.
source: The combination of the structural and physiological data indicates that Mamba1 preferentially binds hASIC1a in a closed state and reduces the proton sensitivity of the channel, representing a closed-state trapping mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing pH-dependent activation curves.

claim: Mamba1 inhibits hASIC1a through a closed-state trapping mechanism.
source: The combination of the structural and physiological data indicates that Mamba1 preferentially binds hASIC1a in a closed state and reduces the proton sensitivity of the channel, representing a closed-state trapping mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by integration of structural and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: ASICs are a group of voltage-independent proton-gated cation channels belonging to the degenerin/epithelial sodium channel (DEG/ENaC) superfamily.
source: Acid-sensing ion channels (ASICs) are a group of voltage-independent proton-gated cation channels belonging to the degenerin/epithelial sodium channel (DEG/ENaC) superfamily (Kellenberger and Schild, 2002; Krishtal and Pidoplichko, 1981; Waldmann et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: ASICs are involved in learning and memory.
source: These channels are involved in diverse physiological processes, including learning and memory (Kreple et al., 2014; Wemmie et al., 2002; Yu et al., 2018), neurodegeneration after ischemic stroke (Gao et al., 2005; Lee and Chen, 2018; Qiang et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2004), and pain sensation (Callejo et al., 2015; Deval et al., 2010; Deval et al., 2011; Wemmie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ASICs are involved in neurodegeneration after ischemic stroke.
source: These channels are involved in diverse physiological processes, including learning and memory (Kreple et al., 2014; Wemmie et al., 2002; Yu et al., 2018), neurodegeneration after ischemic stroke (Gao et al., 2005; Lee and Chen, 2018; Qiang et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2004), and pain sensation (Callejo et al., 2015; Deval et al., 2010; Deval et al., 2011; Wemmie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ASICs are involved in pain sensation.
source: These channels are involved in diverse physiological processes, including learning and memory (Kreple et al., 2014; Wemmie et al., 2002; Yu et al., 2018), neurodegeneration after ischemic stroke (Gao et al., 2005; Lee and Chen, 2018; Qiang et al., 2018; Xiong et al., 2004), and pain sensation (Callejo et al., 2015; Deval et al., 2010; Deval et al., 2011; Wemmie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: ASICs have emerged as potential therapeutic targets in the management of psychiatric disorders, neurodegenerative diseases and pain.
source: Therefore, ASICs have emerged as potential therapeutic targets in the management of psychiatric disorders, neurodegenerative diseases and pain (Baron and Lingueglia, 2015; Rash, 2017; Wemmie et al., 2006; Wemmie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Peptide toxins from venom are the most potent and subtype-selective ASIC modulators.
source: Peptide toxins from venom are the most potent and subtype-selective ASIC modulators and thus have been very powerful tools for studying the gating and modulation mechanisms of ASICs (Baron et al., 2013; Kalia et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Structures of chicken ASIC1 (cASIC1) in different states have been reported in the past decade.
source: In the past decade, structures of chicken ASIC1 (cASIC1) in different states have been reported.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: The structure of apo-form cASIC1 in the inactive state has been reported.
source: These include structures of the apo-form cASIC1 in the inactive (Jasti et al., 2007), desensitized (Gonzales et al., 2009) and resting (Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018) states and of venom-bound states: the MitTx-bound open state (Baconguis et al., 2014), and the PcTx1-bound ion-selective, nonselective (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012), and inactive states (Dawson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jasti et al., 2007.

claim: The structure of apo-form cASIC1 in the desensitized state has been reported.
source: These include structures of the apo-form cASIC1 in the inactive (Jasti et al., 2007), desensitized (Gonzales et al., 2009) and resting (Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018) states and of venom-bound states: the MitTx-bound open state (Baconguis et al., 2014), and the PcTx1-bound ion-selective, nonselective (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012), and inactive states (Dawson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gonzales et al., 2009.

claim: The structure of apo-form cASIC1 in the resting state has been reported.
source: These include structures of the apo-form cASIC1 in the inactive (Jasti et al., 2007), desensitized (Gonzales et al., 2009) and resting (Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018) states and of venom-bound states: the MitTx-bound open state (Baconguis et al., 2014), and the PcTx1-bound ion-selective, nonselective (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012), and inactive states (Dawson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yoder and Gouaux, 2020 and Yoder et al., 2018.

claim: The structure of MitTx-bound cASIC1 in the open state has been reported.
source: These include structures of the apo-form cASIC1 in the inactive (Jasti et al., 2007), desensitized (Gonzales et al., 2009) and resting (Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018) states and of venom-bound states: the MitTx-bound open state (Baconguis et al., 2014), and the PcTx1-bound ion-selective, nonselective (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012), and inactive states (Dawson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Baconguis et al., 2014.

claim: The structure of PcTx1-bound cASIC1 in ion-selective and nonselective states has been reported.
source: These include structures of the apo-form cASIC1 in the inactive (Jasti et al., 2007), desensitized (Gonzales et al., 2009) and resting (Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018) states and of venom-bound states: the MitTx-bound open state (Baconguis et al., 2014), and the PcTx1-bound ion-selective, nonselective (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012), and inactive states (Dawson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012.

claim: The structure of PcTx1-bound cASIC1 in the inactive state has been reported.
source: These include structures of the apo-form cASIC1 in the inactive (Jasti et al., 2007), desensitized (Gonzales et al., 2009) and resting (Yoder and Gouaux, 2020; Yoder et al., 2018) states and of venom-bound states: the MitTx-bound open state (Baconguis et al., 2014), and the PcTx1-bound ion-selective, nonselective (Baconguis and Gouaux, 2012), and inactive states (Dawson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dawson et al., 2012.

claim: In the resting state, the position of the thumb domain lies farther away from the threefold molecular axis, thereby expanding the 'acidic pocket'.
source: In the resting state, the position of the thumb domain lies farther away from the threefold molecular axis, thereby expanding the 'acidic pocket' (Yoder et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yoder et al., 2018.

claim: In the open and desensitized states, the 'closure' of the thumb domain into the acidic pocket expands the lower palm domain, leading to an iris-like opening of the channel gate.
source: In the open and desensitized states, the 'closure' of the thumb domain into the acidic pocket expands the lower palm domain (Baconguis et al., 2014; Gonzales et al., 2009), leading to an iris-like opening of the channel gate.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baconguis et al., 2014 and Gonzales et al., 2009.

claim: Mambalgin1 (Mamba1) is a 57-residue three-finger toxin isolated from the venom of the black mamba snake (Dendroaspis polylepis polylepis).
source: Mambalgin1 (Mamba1), a 57-residue three-finger toxin isolated from the venom of the black mamba snake (Dendroaspis polylepis polylepis), has been proven to be a potent, rapid and reversible inhibitor of ASIC1a- or ASIC1b-containing channels in both central and peripheral neurons (Diochot et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Diochot et al., 2012.

claim: Mamba1 has been proven to be a potent, rapid and reversible inhibitor of ASIC1a- or ASIC1b-containing channels in both central and peripheral neurons.
source: Mambalgin1 (Mamba1), a 57-residue three-finger toxin isolated from the venom of the black mamba snake (Dendroaspis polylepis polylepis), has been proven to be a potent, rapid and reversible inhibitor of ASIC1a- or ASIC1b-containing channels in both central and peripheral neurons (Diochot et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Diochot et al., 2012.

claim: Mamba1 has an analgesic effect that is as strong as that of morphine but does not involve opioid receptors.
source: Mamba1 has an analgesic effect that is as strong as that of morphine but does not involve opioid receptors, highlighting its potential utility for the management of pain.
evidence: This claim is supported by inference from previous research on Mamba1.

claim: Human ASIC1a (hASIC1a) and cASIC1 have ~89% sequence identity.
source: It should be pointed out that, to date, all ASIC structures solved and gating mechanism reported have been of chicken ASIC1, which can be pharmacologically quite different when compared to human ASIC1a despite ~89% sequence identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence comparison data.

claim: Human ASIC1a (hASIC1a) and cASIC1 exhibit different responses to the channel activity modulation toxin Mamba1.
source: Functional studies have shown that human ASIC1a (hASIC1a) and cASIC1 exhibit different responses to the channel activity modulation toxins Mamba1 (Sun et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sun et al., 2018.

claim: Synthetic Mamba1 inhibits the channel currents of both recombinant hASIC1a and cASIC1 in CHO cells.
source: In our own experiments, synthetic Mamba1 was observed to inhibit the channel currents of both recombinant hASIC1a and cASIC1 in CHO cells (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The IC50 of Mamba1 for hASIC1a is 197.3 ± 37.4 nM.
source: The inhibitory effects of Mamba1 on both full-length hASIC1a and cASIC1 are concentration dependent, with IC50 values of 197.3 ± 37.4 and 123.6 ± 28.5 nM, respectively (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The IC50 of Mamba1 for cASIC1 is 123.6 ± 28.5 nM.
source: The inhibitory effects of Mamba1 on both full-length hASIC1a and cASIC1 are concentration dependent, with IC50 values of 197.3 ± 37.4 and 123.6 ± 28.5 nM, respectively (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: In the presence of 500 nM Mamba1, hASIC1a showed a decrease of 60.4 ± 12.9% in the measured sodium currents.
source: Interestingly, in the presence of 500 nM Mamba1, hASIC1a and cASIC1 showed decreases of 60.4 ± 12.9% and 19.6 ± 6.1% respectively, in the measured sodium currents (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: In the presence of 500 nM Mamba1, cASIC1 showed a decrease of 19.6 ± 6.1% in the measured sodium currents.
source: Interestingly, in the presence of 500 nM Mamba1, hASIC1a and cASIC1 showed decreases of 60.4 ± 12.9% and 19.6 ± 6.1% respectively, in the measured sodium currents (Figure 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: At saturation (10 μM Mamba1), hASIC1a showed a decrease in the measured sodium currents of 78.9 ± 6.2%.
source: At saturation (10 μM Mamba1), hASIC1a and cASIC1 showed decreases in the measured sodium currents of 78.9 ± 6.2% and 31.9 ± 4.7% (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: At saturation (10 μM Mamba1), cASIC1 showed a decrease in the measured sodium currents of 31.9 ± 4.7%.
source: At saturation (10 μM Mamba1), hASIC1a and cASIC1 showed decreases in the measured sodium currents of 78.9 ± 6.2% and 31.9 ± 4.7% (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Mamba1 acts as an inhibitor targeting both hASIC1a and cASIC1, with comparable affinities but different efficacies.
source: These data indicated that Mamba1 acts as an inhibitor targeting both hASIC1a and cASIC1, with comparable affinities but different efficacies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data on IC50 values and inhibition percentages.

claim: Functional and pharmacological differences exist between chicken ASIC1 and human ASIC1a.
source: These observations suggested that functional and pharmacological differences exist between chicken ASIC1 and human ASIC1a, thus leading to the question of whether the structures of cASIC1 can fully recapitulate the functional states of hASIC1a.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the different responses of hASIC1a and cASIC1 to Mamba1.

claim: Truncated hASIC1a with the 60 carboxyl terminal residues removed (hASIC1aΔC) is functional.
source: To facilitate the expression and purification of hASIC1a, a series of truncations of full-length hASIC1a was performed. Finally, truncated hASIC1a with the 60 carboxyl terminal residues removed (named hASIC1aΔC) was determined to be functional by whole-cell patch-clamp electrophysiology.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data.

claim: The hASIC1aΔC channel exhibits electrophysiological properties very similar to those of the full-length channel.
source: The hASIC1aΔC channel exhibits electrophysiological properties very similar to those of the full-length channel (Figure 1c–d).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1c-d.

claim: Mamba1 inhibits hASIC1aΔC channels with an IC50 of 106.6 ± 23.6 nM.
source: Mamba1 inhibits hASIC1aΔC channels with an IC50 of 106.6 ± 23.6 nM, which is comparable to the reported IC50 of full-length hASIC1a in CHO cells (148.6 ± 33.2 nM) (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The trimeric hASIC1aΔC shows a canonical chalice-like architecture.
source: The trimeric hASIC1aΔC shows a canonical chalice-like architecture (Figure 2a–b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 2a-b.

claim: Each subunit of hASIC1aΔC harbors a cysteine-rich extracellular domain (ECD).
source: Each subunit of hASIC1aΔC harbors a cysteine-rich extracellular domain (ECD).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data.

claim: The ECD resembles a hand-like architecture with the palm, knuckle, finger and thumb domains clenching a 'ball' of β strands.
source: The ECD resembles a hand-like architecture with the palm, knuckle, finger and thumb domains clenching a 'ball' of β strands (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: In the transmembrane domain (TMD) of hASIC1aΔC, two transmembrane helices, TM1 and TM2, are observed to connect to the β1 and β12 strands of the palm domain at a juncture called the 'wrist'.
source: In the transmembrane domain (TMD) of hASIC1aΔC, two transmembrane helices, TM1 and TM2, are observed to connect to the β1 and β12 strands of the palm domain at a juncture called the 'wrist' (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: TM2 is not a continuous α-helix but rather has a break in the helical structure.
source: The density map of TM2 provides convincing evidence that the helix is not a continuous α-helix but rather has a break in the helical structure (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the density map shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The helical structure of TM2 ends at Ile443 and resumes at Ile447.
source: The helical structure of TM2 ends at Ile443 and resumes at Ile447.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data.

claim: Residues Gly444, Ala445, and Ser446 adopt a nonhelical conformation, dividing TM2 into segments TM2a and TM2b.
source: Residues Gly444, Ala445, and Ser446 adopt a nonhelical conformation, dividing TM2 into segments TM2a and TM2b.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data.

claim: The TM2b helical element interacts with the cytoplasmic portion of TM1 of the adjacent subunit.
source: The TM2b helical element interacts with the cytoplasmic portion of TM1 of the adjacent subunit (Figure 2c), resulting in a swap of the TM2 helices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The three copies of TM1, TM2a and TM2b define a cavernous, threefold symmetric pore of the hASIC1a channel.
source: Overall, the three copies of TM1, TM2a and TM2b define a cavernous, threefold symmetric pore of the hASIC1a channel, in which TM2 resides on the periphery of the pore (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The ion channel pore of hASIC1aΔC harbors a modest negative potential conferred by the presence of Asp434 and Gln438, by the carbonyl oxygen atoms of Gly437, Gly440, and Gly444.
source: Electrostatic mapping of the solvent-accessible surface reveals that the ion channel pore of hASIC1aΔC harbors a modest negative potential conferred by the presence of Asp434 and Gln438, by the carbonyl oxygen atoms of Gly437, Gly440, and Gly444 (Figure 2e).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrostatic mapping shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The pore profile of hASIC1aΔC shows a closed gate along the threefold axis as a result of primary constrictions at Asp434 and Gly437.
source: The pore profile of hASIC1aΔC also shows a closed gate along the threefold axis as a result of primary constrictions at Asp434 and Gly437 (Figure 2e–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by the pore profile analysis shown in Figure 2e-f.

claim: The apo-hASIC1aΔC structure at pH 8.0 has high similarity with the resting-state structure of cASIC1 at pH 8.0.
source: The apo-hASIC1aΔC structure at pH 8.0 is observed to have high similarity with the resting-state structure of cASIC1 at pH 8.0 (Yoder et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison with cASIC1.

claim: The structures of apo-hASIC1aΔC and resting-state cASIC1 can be well superimposed with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 0.88 Å over 1124 aligned Cα atoms.
source: The two structures can be well superimposed with a root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) of 0.88 Å over 1124 aligned Cα atoms (Figure 2g).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural superposition analysis shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The structure of the acidic pockets of hASIC1aΔC and cASIC1 is almost identical, giving an RMSD of 0.41 Å.
source: Especially, the structure of the acidic pockets of hASIC1aΔC and cASIC1 is almost identical, giving an RMSD of 0.41 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: In the acidic pocket, the distances between the Cα atoms of Asp347-Glu238 and Asp351-Asp237 in hASIC1aΔC are measured to be 13.9 and 15.6 Å, respectively.
source: In the acidic pocket, the distances between the Cα atoms of Asp347-Glu238 and Asp351-Asp237 in hASIC1aΔC are measured to be 13.9 and 15.6 Å, respectively, which are comparable to the distances measured in the cASIC1 channel (13.0 Å for Asp346-Glu239 and 15.0 Å for Asp350-Asp238) (Figure 2g).
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements from the structure shown in Figure 2g.

claim: The distances between the Cα atoms of Asp346-Glu239 and Asp350-Asp238 in cASIC1 are 13.0 Å and 15.0 Å, respectively.
source: In the acidic pocket, the distances between the Cα atoms of Asp347-Glu238 and Asp351-Asp237 in hASIC1aΔC are measured to be 13.9 and 15.6 Å, respectively, which are comparable to the distances measured in the cASIC1 channel (13.0 Å for Asp346-Glu239 and 15.0 Å for Asp350-Asp238) (Figure 2g).
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements from the cASIC1 structure.

claim: The structures of the TMDs of hASIC1aΔC and cASIC1 are superimposed well, with an RMSD value of 0.34 Å.
source: Moreover, the structures of the TMDs of hASIC1aΔC and cASIC1 are superimposed well, with an RMSD value of 0.34 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural superposition analysis.

claim: The pore profiles of hASIC1aΔC and cASIC1 are almost the same.
source: The pore profiles of hASIC1aΔC and cASIC1 are almost the same (Figure 2f).
evidence: This claim is supported by pore profile analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The structure of hASIC1aΔC reported here represents the resting state of hASIC1a.
source: Combining this information with the electrophysiology data, we conclude that the structure of hASIC1aΔC reported here represents the resting state of hASIC1a.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural and electrophysiological data.

claim: The overall architecture of the hASIC1aΔC-Mamba1 complex shows a triskelion-like shape viewed down the threefold symmetry axis.
source: The overall architecture of the hASIC1aΔC-Mamba1 complex shows a triskelion-like shape viewed down the threefold symmetry axis, with one Mamba1 molecule radiating from each hASIC1aΔC subunit (Figure 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Each of the three Mamba1 molecules binds to the ECD of a subunit of hASIC1aΔC, interacting with the outside of the ECD of hASIC1aΔC.
source: Each of the three Mamba1 molecules binds to the ECD of a subunit of hASIC1aΔC, interacting with the outside of the ECD of hASIC1aΔC (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Mamba1 interacts with the thumb domain of hASIC1a channel.
source: Different with the PcTx1 and MitTx toxins, Mambal1 was observed to interact with the thumb domain of hASIC1a channel.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural data.

claim: The interaction between PcTx1 and cASIC1 involves the thumb, palm and β-ball domains.
source: Although the interaction between PcTx1 and cASIC1 involves the thumb, palm and β-ball domains (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The interaction between MitTx and cASIC1 involves the palm domain besides the thumb domain.
source: The interaction between MitTx and cASIC1 involves the palm domain besides the thumb domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b.

claim: The binding of Mamba1 to hASIC1aΔC induces a conformational change in Finger-II of Mamba1.
source: The binding of Mamba1 to hASIC1aΔC induces a conformational change in Finger-II of Mamba1.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison.

claim: The tip region of Finger-II flips to the thumb domain of hASIC1aΔC to facilitate the interaction between the toxin and the channel.
source: The tip region of Finger-II flips to the thumb domain of hASIC1aΔC to facilitate the interaction between the toxin and the channel (Figure 3—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c.

claim: In the tip region of Finger-II, Arg28 is oriented toward the α5 helix of the thumb domain, thus becoming closer to Asp347 and Asp351.
source: In the tip region of Finger-II, Arg28 is oriented toward the α5 helix of the thumb domain, thus becoming closer to Asp347 and Asp351.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The measured distances between the Cα atoms of Arg28-Asp347 and Arg28-Asp351 are 10.5 and 10.2 Å, respectively.
source: The measured distances between the Cα atoms of Arg28-Asp347 and Arg28-Asp351 are 10.5 and 10.2 Å, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by distance measurements from the structure.

claim: There could be salt bridges between Arg28 and Asp347 or Asp351.
source: Although the side chains of Arg28, Asp347 and Asp351 cannot be clearly assigned, it seems there could be salt bridges between Arg28 and Asp347 or Asp351 (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is speculative based on structural proximity shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Phe352 is nestled within a hydrophobic cluster composed of Met25, Phe27, Leu32 and Leu33 in Finger-II of Mamba1, mediating a hydrophobic interaction between Mamba1 and hASIC1aΔC.
source: Phe352, a residue that is conserved in ASIC1 orthologues, is nestled within a hydrophobic cluster composed of Met25, Phe27, Leu32 and Leu33 in Finger-II of Mamba1, mediating a hydrophobic interaction between Mamba1 and hASIC1aΔC (Figure 3c).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Mamba1 could form multiple polar contacts with hASIC1aΔC through its Finger-I region.
source: Moreover, Mamba1 could form multiple polar contacts with hASIC1aΔC through its Finger-I region.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: Mamba1-Gln5 and His6 could form hydrogen bonds with the side chain of Tyr360 of hASIC1aΔC.
source: Mamba1-Gln5 and His6 could form hydrogen bonds with the side chain of Tyr360 of hASIC1aΔC.
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural proximity.

claim: Mamba1-Lys8 could form salt bridges with Asp300.
source: Mamba1-Lys8 could form salt bridges with Asp300 (Figure 3d).
evidence: This claim is inferred from structural proximity shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Finger-III of Mamba1 is located farther from the thumb domain of hASIC1aΔC, pointing in the opposite direction from the threefold axis of the channel core.
source: Notably, Finger-III of Mamba1 is located farther from the thumb domain of hASIC1aΔC, pointing in the opposite direction from the threefold axis of the channel core.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: Finger-III has no contact with hASIC1aΔC.
source: Finger-III thus has no contact with hASIC1aΔC (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The upper scaffold region of Mamba1 does not contact hASIC1aΔC.
source: The upper scaffold region of Mamba1 likewise does not contact hASIC1aΔC.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The inhibition of hASIC1a activity by Mamba1 is greatly reduced when residue Mamba1-Gln5, His6, Lys8, Phe27 or Arg28 is mutated to Ala.
source: The inhibition of hASIC1a activity by Mamba1 is greatly reduced when residue Mamba1-Gln5, His6, Lys8, Phe27 or Arg28 is mutated to Ala (Figure 3e).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Mamba1 is significantly less effective in inhibiting the hASIC1a mutants Asp347Ala, Asp351Gly, Phe352Leu and Tyr360Ala.
source: Mamba1 is significantly less effective in inhibiting the hASIC1a mutants Asp347Ala, Asp351Gly, Phe352Leu and Tyr360Ala (Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis and electrophysiology data shown in Figure 3f and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: These data are consistent with previous electrophysiological studies on chicken or rat ASIC1 channels.
source: These data are consistent with previous electrophysiological studies on chicken or rat ASIC1 channels (Mourier et al., 2016; Salinas et al., 2014; Sun et al., 2018).

claim: Several key amino acid differences between hASIC1a and cASIC1, including Arg155 and the Glu102-Asp165 pair in hASIC1a (corresponding to Leu156 and Arg103-Glu168 in cASIC1, respectively), are found to contribute to the different responses of hASIC1a and cASIC1 to Mamba1.

claim: ASIC channels are of fundamental importance and are also considered potential drug targets in therapeutic interventions against pain and ischemic stroke.

claim: Analysis of interactions between venom toxin and hASIC1a or peptide toxin-based drug development should follow structure and function studies on human source target proteins.
source: There is no doubt that analysis of interactions between venom toxin and hASIC1a or peptide toxin-based drug development should follow structure and function studies on human source target proteins, as data on homologous target proteins from other species might not precisely reflect the modulatory effects of the peptide or of other ligands on the target proteins, which will strongly influence the process of drug development for human target proteins.
evidence: This claim is an opinion based on the findings of the study.

claim: This is the first structure of human ASICs.
source: In this study, we resolved the cryo-EM structures of hASIC1a in the apo-form and in complex with the Mamba1 toxin at 3.56 Å and 3.90 Å resolution representing the first structure of human ASICs, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by the novelty of the structural determination.
